claims.text: Kahn published Topological sorting of large networks in Communications of the ACM, volume 5 number 11, pages 558 to 562, in November 1962. The paper states that topological sorting is a procedure required for many problems involving analysis of networks, giving the project scheduling technique of the period as an example.

source.title: Kahn, A. B., Topological sorting of large networks, Communications of the ACM 5(11):558-562, November 1962

claims.text: The paper presents a general method permitting treatment of larger networks than existing procedures and with greater efficiency, discussed in terms of a contemporary machine, and reports that a network of 30,000 activities can be ordered in less than one hour of machine time.

source.title: Kahn, A. B., Topological sorting of large networks, Communications of the ACM 5(11):558-562, November 1962

claims.text: The method was developed as a byproduct of a procedure needed at Westinghouse, where Kahn worked, and was never programmed.

source.title: Kahn, A. B., Topological sorting of large networks, Communications of the ACM 5(11):558-562, November 1962

claims.text: The algorithm now bearing Kahn’s name repeatedly removes vertices having no incoming edges, adding them to the order in the sequence removed; removing a vertex also removes its outgoing edges, which exposes a new set of vertices with no incoming edges, and the procedure repeats until no vertices remain.

source.title: Kahn, A. B., Topological sorting of large networks, Communications of the ACM 5(11):558-562, November 1962

claims.text: A caveat on the record: the journal’s current landing page for this article displays a mismatched abstract about pattern classification, apparently a metadata error, while the digital library entry carries the correct one.

source.title: Kahn, A. B., Topological sorting of large networks, Communications of the ACM 5(11):558-562, November 1962

beats.broke: things depend on other things, and you need a single order to do them in — but the dependencies are a graph and an order is a line
beats.fix: repeatedly take anything with nothing left to wait for, which is possible exactly as long as something is waiting for nothing
beats.cost: the procedure only terminates with everything ordered if the graph has no cycles, so the algorithm is also the cycle test and there is no separate check to skip
beats.interview: what it means when a topological sort stops with vertices left over
